options: Unspecified values, because the last two elements are not initialized
Nothing: the initializer has too few elements and the program is ill-formed
questions.explanation: `std::array` is an aggregate, so aggregate initialization applies: elements without an initializer are value-initialized, which gives zero for `int`. This is the same as for a built-in array. Indeterminate values only appear when the array is declared with no initializer at all, as in `std::array<int, 4> a;`.

The string is read with its rightmost character as bit 0, the way a binary literal is written, so `"0110"` has bit 1 and bit 2 set and the value is 6. That makes `b[1]` equal to 1 and `b[0]` equal to 0, printed as `10`. Reading the string left to right as indices 0 to 3 gives the reversed answers.

options: Undefined behavior: `v[0]` returns a dangling reference
Ill-formed: `auto` cannot deduce the proxy type
questions.explanation: `v[0]` on a non-const `vector<bool>` returns a proxy object of type `vector<bool>::reference`, and `auto` copies the proxy, not the bit. The proxy still refers to element 0 of the vector, which is now false, and it converts to `0` when printed. The proxy would dangle only if the vector were reallocated or destroyed.

Dereferencing a `vector<bool>` iterator yields a prvalue proxy, and a non-const lvalue reference cannot bind to a prvalue, so `auto&` in (2) is rejected. By-value `auto` copies the proxy, a forwarding reference binds to the prvalue, and `const auto&` extends its lifetime. Loop (3) is the portable way to write generic code that modifies elements.

questions.prompt: Both threads write different elements of each vector, and the vectors are not resized. Which has a data race?
options: Neither: the threads write different elements
questions.explanation: The standard lets different elements of a container be modified concurrently, with an explicit exception for `vector<bool>`. Its elements share words, so a write to one bit is a read-modify-write of storage that holds its neighbours, and two such writes race. The `vector<char>` elements are distinct memory locations and are safe. Use `vector<char>` or a vector of atomics, or add a lock, if threads share a boolean vector.

options: `10`, because `a` was rebound to the element `b` refers to
questions.explanation: Assigning one `vector<bool>::reference` to another copies the bit it refers to into the bit it refers to, as an assignment of the values would, and does not rebind it. So `a = b` stores false into element 0, which makes both elements false. The tempting `10` treats the proxy like a pointer that can be reseated, but like a real reference it stays attached to its element.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `std::vector<bool>` does the C++23 standard guarantee?
options: `operator[]` on a non-const `vector<bool>` returns a value of a class type, `vector<bool>::reference`
Each element is stored in exactly one bit
`v.data()` returns a pointer to the packed words
questions.explanation: The standard declares `vector<bool>::reference` as a class with a conversion to `bool`, assignment from `bool` and a `flip` member, and that class is what `operator[]` returns. Space optimization is only the motivation: bit packing is not mandated, no `data()` exists, and no size comparison is promised, although every major implementation packs bits.

questions.prompt: Assume `unsigned long` has 64 bits. What does the standard say happens here?
options: It returns the low bits, ignoring bit 70
Undefined behavior: the value does not fit
questions.explanation: `to_ulong` throws `std::overflow_error` if the value cannot be represented as an `unsigned long`, and bit 70 is set, which cannot fit in a 64-bit `unsigned long`. It does not truncate. A bitset of 100 bits with only low bits set converts without any problem, so the check is on the value and not on the template size.
